rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Uterosacral nodularity**, fixed retroverted uterus, posterior cul-de-sac tenderness
Dyschezia or cyclic rectal bleeding → bowel involvement; urinary cyclic symptoms → bladder disease
Pain severity poorly correlates with lesion burden; examination may be normal

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Estrogen-responsive implants provoke inflammation, fibrosis, adhesions, and distortion of pelvic anatomy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical assessment + **transvaginal ultrasound** first; normal imaging cannot exclude superficial disease
MRI maps deep lesions or indeterminate adnexal masses; CA-125 not a diagnostic test
★ **Laparoscopy with biopsy**: definitive test; for uncertain diagnosis, refractory symptoms, or planned operative treatment
Current ACOG: presumptive clinical diagnosis, no surgery before empiric treatment; older exams may expect laparoscopy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Pain, no immediate pregnancy goal → **NSAID + continuous combined OCP** or progestin
Persistent symptoms → GnRH agonist/antagonist with add-back hormones to limit hypoestrogenic adverse effects
Refractory disease or selected infertility → laparoscopic excision/ablation and adhesiolysis
Endometrioma surgery may reduce ovarian reserve; balance pain, suspicion, size, and fertility goals
Trying to conceive → fertility evaluation; hormonal suppression does not improve spontaneous conception

rows.label: Complications
items: Adhesive infertility, bowel/ureteral obstruction, chronic pain; small increase in clear-cell/endometrioid ovarian cancer
GnRH suppression → hot flashes, bone loss; disease may recur after conservative surgery

rows.label: Prevention
items: Postoperative hormonal suppression reduces pain recurrence when pregnancy not desired; no established primary prevention

rows.label: Mimics
items: Adenomyosis: diffusely enlarged, boggy uterus with heavy bleeding
PID: fever, discharge, cervical motion tenderness; pain less cyclic
Primary dysmenorrhea: normal examination, onset soon after menarche, no structural lesion

table.title: Anatomic forms
rows: Fibrotic nodules involving ligaments, bowel, bladder
Ovarian chocolate cyst; homogeneous ground-glass ultrasound echoes

enterovirus-infections.name: Enterovirus infections
enterovirus-infections.scope: Coxsackievirus A, Coxsackievirus B (epidemic pleurodynia, viral myocarditis, pericarditis), echovirus, aseptic meningitis
enterovirus-infections.core: Enteroviruses cause common self-limited febrile syndromes but also aseptic meningitis, myocarditis and severe neonatal sepsis-like illness.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young children, summer/early autumn, childcare exposure; fecal–oral and respiratory spread
Newborn peripartum exposure and antibody deficiency increase severe disseminated infection risk

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Hand-foot-mouth: oral ulcers plus **vesicles on palms/soles**; sometimes buttocks
Herpangina: fever with painful **posterior oropharyngeal vesicles/ulcers**, usually no hand/foot eruption
Pleurodynia: paroxysmal chest/upper abdominal muscle spasms, fever, **elevated CK**
Neonates: poor feeding, hepatitis, coagulopathy, shock or arrhythmia; older children: headache/meningismus

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Nonenveloped positive-sense RNA picornaviruses survive gastric acidity; replication followed by viremia
Tissue tropism produces mucocutaneous, meningeal, myocardial or skeletal muscle disease

rows.label: Dx
items: Typical uncomplicated exanthem → clinical diagnosis; no routine serology
★ Suspected meningitis → **LP with CSF enterovirus PCR**, bacterial studies and glucose/protein
Viral CSF usually lymphocytic, normal glucose, mildly elevated protein; early neutrophils possible
Chest pain with cardiac concern → ECG, troponin, echocardiography; MRI for suspected myocarditis
Ill neonate → blood/CSF cultures and sepsis evaluation; do not assume benign viral disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Uncomplicated disease → **oral fluids, acetaminophen/ibuprofen**, assess hydration
Unexcluded bacterial meningitis/sepsis → empiric ceftriaxone + vancomycin; neonates → ampicillin + cefotaxime
Myocarditis → cardiac monitoring, heart-failure support; shock → intensive care and circulatory support
No routine antibiotic or antiviral treatment for confirmed uncomplicated enterovirus infection
Painful mouth lesions → cool liquids; avoid aspirin in children

rows.label: Complications
items: Dehydration, myopericarditis, encephalitis; some serotypes cause acute flaccid myelitis
Fulminant neonatal hepatitis/coagulopathy or myocardial failure can be fatal

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Handwashing with soap, surface cleaning, diaper hygiene; viral stool shedding can persist
Routine polio vaccination prevents poliomyelitis; no routine US vaccine for nonpolio enteroviruses

rows.label: Mimics
items: HSV gingivostomatitis: anterior diffuse gingivitis and painful lesions
Bacterial meningitis: low CSF glucose, high protein; cultures/PCR establish cause
Pulmonary embolism: hypoxemia, clot risk; viral pleurisy → fever, **pleural friction rub**, viral rash
Streptococcal pharyngitis: tonsillar exudates, palatal petechiae, no discrete vesicles

enterovirus-infections.evidence: Not checked online; established infectious-disease teaching.

epididymitis.name: Epididymitis
epididymitis.scope: Acute epididymitis, sexually transmitted vs enteric pathogens by age, Prehn sign, empiric antibiotic regimens, ruling out torsion
epididymitis.core: Gradual unilateral posterior testicular pain with urinary or urethral inflammation suggests epididymitis; always assess for torsion first.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sexually active younger adults: gonorrhea/chlamydia; older adults with obstruction/instrumentation: enteric organisms
Insertive anal intercourse permits both STI and enteric pathogens; exposure matters more than age

rows.label: Clues
items: Tender swollen epididymis, dysuria, fever, possible urethral discharge; cremasteric reflex often preserved
Prehn sign: elevation may relieve pain, but **cannot exclude torsion**
Sudden severe onset, nausea, high-riding/horizontal testis → surgical emergency

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ascending urethral/urinary infection spreads through vas deferens → epididymal inflammation
Extension into testis causes epididymo-orchitis; edema can impair perfusion in severe disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ High torsion suspicion → **urgent urology/exploration**, without waiting for testing
Uncertain → **Doppler ultrasound**; epididymal hyperemia favors infection, absent testicular flow favors torsion
★ First-catch urine **gonorrhea/chlamydia NAAT**, urinalysis, bacterial urine culture; HIV/syphilis testing
Negative ultrasound does not exclude epididymitis; persistent mass warrants alternative-diagnosis evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Empiric antibiotics after specimens; **scrotal support, NSAIDs**, relative rest
Treat before test results; regimen determined by likely pathogens, not age alone
Reevaluate if no improvement within **72 hours**; severe fever/pain or inability to adhere → hospitalization

rows.label: Complications
items: Abscess, testicular infarction, chronic scrotal pain, reduced fertility
Persistent swelling after treatment → assess tumor, TB, abscess, infarction

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ STI-associated infection: **partners from prior 60 days** need evaluation/presumptive treatment
Abstain until both partners treated and symptoms resolved; condoms reduce reinfection

rows.label: Mimics
items: Testicular torsion: abrupt pain, absent reflex; urgent detorsion required
Torsed appendage: focal upper-pole tenderness, blue-dot sign
Inguinal hernia: groin/scrotal mass, bowel symptoms, reducibility or strangulation

esophageal-atresia-and-tracheoesophageal.name: Esophageal atresia and tracheoesophageal fistula
esophageal-atresia-and-tracheoesophageal.scope: Esophageal atresia, tracheoesophageal fistula types, VACTERL association, coiled nasogastric tube on chest x-ray
esophageal-atresia-and-tracheoesophageal.core: A newborn with excessive oral secretions, choking and cyanosis during feeds requires evaluation for esophageal atresia or tracheoesophageal fistula.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prenatal polyhydramnios and small/absent stomach bubble suggest impaired fetal swallowing
Associated anomalies: **VACTERL**—vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb defects

rows.label: Clues
items: Frothy drooling, feeding-associated respiratory distress, recurrent desaturation or aspiration
★ **Nasogastric/orogastric tube cannot pass** into stomach; avoid repeated forceful attempts
Abdominal distention suggests airway-to-stomach communication; isolated atresia often has gasless abdomen
H-type fistula: esophagus patent, delayed recurrent pneumonia or cough with liquids

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Abnormal foregut separation leaves esophageal discontinuity and/or connection to trachea
Secretions pool proximally; distal communication permits reflux aspiration and gastric inflation during ventilation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Gentle radiopaque tube placement → **chest/abdominal radiograph showing proximal coiling**
Distal bowel gas supports distal fistula; absent gas favors no distal connection
Routine contrast feeding unnecessary in classic atresia; aspiration can worsen lung injury
Suspected H-type → carefully supervised contrast esophagram and bronchoscopy
Echocardiography before surgery; assess anus, kidneys, spine and limbs for associated anomalies

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO, head elevation, continuous proximal pouch suction**, IV fluids and pediatric surgical referral
Secure airway if respiratory failure; minimize bag-mask ventilation because fistula can inflate stomach
★ Definitive → **fistula ligation and esophageal anastomosis** after stabilization
Long-gap atresia → staged nutritional and reconstructive plan; aspiration pneumonia → IV antibiotics
Feeding resumed after postoperative assessment of repair integrity and swallowing safety

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, anastomotic leak/stricture, recurrent fistula, reflux and dysmotility
Associated tracheomalacia can cause persistent noisy breathing, cyanotic spells or recurrent respiratory infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Prenatal recognition enables delivery planning; aspiration precautions until repaired
Long-term monitoring for dysphagia, reflux, growth failure and recurrent respiratory symptoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: Choanal atresia: cyanosis improves with crying; nasal catheter obstructed
Laryngeal cleft: aspiration with patent esophagus
Pyloric stenosis: later nonbilious vomiting without tube coiling

table.title: Anatomic patterns
rows: Most common; proximal pouch + bowel gas

esophageal-atresia-and-tracheoesophageal.evidence: Not checked online; established neonatal surgical teaching.

essential-hypertension.name: Essential hypertension
essential-hypertension.scope: Blood pressure staging, nonpharmacologic interventions (weight loss, DASH, exercise), first-line antihypertensive agents, resistant hypertension
essential-hypertension.core: Persistently elevated arterial pressure usually reflects multifactorial primary hypertension; confirm accurate repeated measurements before long-term treatment decisions.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, family history, obesity, excess sodium/alcohol, inactivity, poor sleep
NSAIDs, stimulants, oral contraceptives can raise BP; assess before labeling primary disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually asymptomatic; headache alone does not establish hypertensive emergency
★ **Acute target-organ injury** with severe pressure → hypertensive emergency; BP number alone insufficient

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Increased vascular resistance, altered renal sodium handling, sympathetic/RAAS activation sustain elevated pressure
Chronic endothelial injury accelerates atherosclerosis and small-vessel organ damage
Older adults: large-artery stiffness (low compliance) → **isolated systolic hypertension**, wide pulse pressure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Average ≥2 readings on ≥2 visits; confirm using **home BP or ambulatory monitoring**
Rest seated, feet supported, correct cuff, arm at heart level; avoid recent caffeine/exercise
BMP, creatinine/eGFR, urinalysis/albuminuria, lipids, glucose/A1c, ECG assess risk and injury
Resistant: above goal on 3 agents including diuretic, or controlled on ≥4; exclude pseudoresistance
Child/adolescent high oscillometric reading → **confirm by auscultation** before ambulatory monitoring or workup

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **DASH diet, weight reduction, sodium restriction, aerobic activity**, moderate alcohol; target generally <130/80
≥140/90 → drugs, usually two classes; ≥130/80 with CVD, diabetes, CKD, or PREVENT ≥7.5% → drugs
★ Low-risk stage 1: **3–6 months lifestyle**, then drugs if still ≥130/80; updated 2025 threshold
Initial: chlorthalidone, amlodipine, lisinopril, or losartan; albuminuric CKD → ACE inhibitor/ARB (older exams: any diabetes)
Resistant after optimized triple regimen → spironolactone; monitor K/creatinine; never combine ACE inhibitor + ARB

rows.label: Complications
items: Stroke, MI, LV hypertrophy/HF, CKD, retinopathy, aortic disease
Thiazide: low Na/K, gout; ACE inhibitor: cough/angioedema; RAAS drugs contraindicated in pregnancy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication adherence, home readings, regular follow-up; assess orthostatic symptoms in older adults
Weight loss: largest lifestyle BP drop, ~1 mm Hg/kg; smoking cessation barely lowers resting BP
BP control: largest modifiable stroke-risk reduction; also prevents concentric LVH and HF

rows.label: Mimics
items: White-coat hypertension: office high, home normal
Masked hypertension: elevated out-of-office only; secondary causes: abrupt/refractory pressure with renal/endocrine clues

foodborne-illnesses.name: Foodborne illnesses
foodborne-illnesses.scope: Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin, Bacillus cereus, Clostridium perfringens, scombroid, ciguatera, Salmonella, Campylobacter
foodborne-illnesses.core: Incubation time and the dominant symptom separate preformed-toxin vomiting from intestinal infection requiring selective stool testing and antibiotics.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Food improperly refrigerated/reheated; shared-meal outbreaks; raw poultry/eggs, unpasteurized dairy, undercooked meat
Infancy, older age, immunosuppression or vascular disease increase invasive Salmonella risk
Improperly chilled tuna/mackerel → scombroid; tropical reef fish → ciguatera

rows.label: Clues
items: Abrupt short-lived emesis without fever favors ingested toxin; inflammatory enteritis → fever or bloody stools
★ **Severe dehydration, bacteremia signs or persistent bloody diarrhea** → urgent assessment
Campylobacter pain may mimic appendicitis; poultry exposure supports both major invasive enteric pathogens
Fish toxins: scombroid → flushing/urticaria; ciguatera → paresthesias, hot/cold temperature reversal

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ingested enterotoxins act rapidly; scombroid: histamine; ciguatoxin activates voltage-gated sodium channels
Invasive mucosal infection induces inflammation and can permit bloodstream spread
S aureus: **heat-stable** preformed enterotoxin builds in unrefrigerated food; cooking does not destroy it

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Mild brief outbreak illness → **clinical diagnosis**, usually no stool studies
Fever, bloody/mucoid stool, severe tenderness or sepsis → stool PCR/culture including Shiga toxin testing
Suspected bacteremia → blood cultures; report suspected outbreaks to public health

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Scombroid → **diphenhydramine/famotidine**; anaphylaxis → epinephrine; ciguatera → supportive care
Oral rehydration; severe dehydration → IV isotonic fluids; toxin syndromes do not benefit from antibiotics
Campylobacter severe/prolonged or high-risk illness → azithromycin; most mild cases resolve untreated
Nontyphoidal Salmonella: severe/invasive or high-risk host → ceftriaxone or susceptibility-directed antibiotic
★ Suspected **STEC → avoid antibiotics and antimotility drugs**; hemolytic uremic syndrome risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Campylobacter → Guillain-Barré, reactive arthritis; Salmonella → bacteremia, vascular infection, sickle-cell osteomyelitis
Volume depletion → AKI; antibiotics may prolong uncomplicated Salmonella carriage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Cook poultry/eggs thoroughly; separate raw foods, rapid refrigeration, handwashing; avoid unpasteurized products

rows.label: Mimics
items: Norovirus: contagious outbreak with vomiting and diarrhea
Appendicitis: focal progressive peritoneal findings; toxin illness usually self-limited

foodborne-illnesses.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [CDC marine toxins](https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/environmental-hazards-risks/food-poisoning-from-marine-toxins.html), CDC Salmonella/Campylobacter and IDSA infectious-diarrhea guidance.

table.title: Timing after exposure
rows: Vomiting; cream pastries, mayonnaise salads, handled meats

gallstone-disease.name: Gallstone disease
gallstone-disease.scope: Biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, cholangitis, gallstone pancreatitis
gallstone-disease.core: Gallstone location determines the syndrome: transient cystic obstruction, gallbladder inflammation, common-duct obstruction/infection, or pancreatic inflammation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, female sex, pregnancy, obesity, rapid weight loss, ileal disease/resection
Hemolysis/cirrhosis → pigment stones; critical illness/TPN → acalculous cholecystitis

rows.label: Clues
items: Postprandial RUQ/epigastric discomfort radiating to back or right shoulder; assess fever and jaundice
★ **Fever + RUQ pain + jaundice** → cholangitis; hypotension/confusion → severe infection
Pancreatitis: persistent epigastric pain radiating to back, vomiting; ALT >150 supports biliary cause

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cholesterol supersaturation or pigment precipitation creates calculi; obstruction location dictates organ injury
Infected obstructed bile ducts require drainage because antibiotics cannot reliably sterilize a closed system

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **RUQ ultrasound first**; CBC, bilirubin/alkaline phosphatase, AST/ALT, lipase
Suspected cholecystitis with equivocal ultrasound → HIDA; nonvisualized gallbladder supports cystic-duct obstruction
Intermediate common-duct stone probability → MRCP or EUS; ERCP reserved primarily for treatment
★ Direct intervention: **stone seen, cholangitis, or bilirubin >4 mg/dL plus dilated duct**
Post-cholecystectomy jaundice + dilated ducts → retained stone/duct injury → **ERCP**; HIDA only for bile leak

rows.label: Tx
items: Analgesia, fluids, antiemetics; infection → ceftriaxone/metronidazole or piperacillin/tazobactam
★ **Cholangitis → urgent biliary drainage**, immediately after stabilization if shock; do not await antibiotic response
Poor surgical candidate with acute cholecystitis → percutaneous cholecystostomy
★ Gallstone pancreatitis → supportive care, early oral feeding; **no urgent ERCP without cholangitis/persistent obstruction**

rows.label: Complications
items: Empyema, gangrene, perforation, abscess, septic shock; pancreatitis → necrosis/organ failure
Cholecystoenteric fistula → gallstone ileus; imaging: bowel obstruction, pneumobilia, ectopic stone
ERCP → pancreatitis/bleeding/perforation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain healthy weight; avoid rapid weight loss; selected bariatric patients → ursodiol prophylaxis
After duct clearance → cholecystectomy; after mild biliary pancreatitis → same-admission cholecystectomy
Asymptomatic uncomplicated stones → observation; no routine prophylactic surgery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hepatitis: marked aminotransferase elevation, no obstructing stone
PUD: burning epigastric pain, ulcer on endoscopy
Inferior MI: ischemic ECG/troponin changes, cardiovascular risk

table.title: Localizing obstruction
rows: Persistent >6 hours, Murphy sign, wall thickening
Cholestatic labs, duct stone/dilation; no infection
ERCP extraction or operative duct clearance
Inflamed gallbladder without stones; critically ill

gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.scope: Clinical diagnosis, empiric PPI trial, lifestyle measures, alarm symptoms, Barrett esophagus screening, 24-hour pH monitoring
gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.core: Heartburn and acid regurgitation after meals or recumbency suggest reflux; complications or diagnostic uncertainty change the testing pathway.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Obesity, pregnancy, hiatal hernia, smoking; drugs reducing lower esophageal sphincter tone
Late large meals and individual food triggers exacerbate symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: Sour taste, nocturnal symptoms, chest discomfort; chronic nocturnal/supine cough may be sole symptom
★ **Dysphagia, odynophagia, bleeding, weight loss**, persistent vomiting, anemia → endoscopy
Exertional chest pain → cardiac evaluation; nocturnal burning relieved upright → empiric acid suppression
Infant spit-up + **poor weight gain** → pathologic GERD; pyloric stenosis: projectile vomiting at 3–6 weeks

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transient lower sphincter relaxation and impaired barrier allow gastric contents into esophagus
Acid exposure → erosions; chronic injury may produce intestinal metaplasia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical symptoms without alarms → **8-week empiric once-daily PPI trial**
Alarm features or failed treatment → upper endoscopy; biopsies evaluate alternative mucosal disease
★ Unproven GERD + normal endoscopy → **ambulatory pH monitoring off PPI**
Proven GERD with refractory symptoms → impedance-pH testing on PPI after optimizing use
Manometry evaluates motility and precedes antireflux surgery; not the primary reflux diagnostic test

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Omeprazole 30–60 minutes before breakfast**; verify adherence before escalation
Intermittent mild symptoms → antacid or famotidine; persistent breakthrough → optimize/split PPI schedule
Weight reduction if overweight; avoid meals within 2–3 hours of bedtime, elevate bed head
Objective reflux with regurgitation or **recurrent aspiration** despite drugs → fundoplication; gastrostomy alone inadequate
Severe erosive esophagitis → long-term PPI or surgery; step down uncomplicated controlled disease

rows.label: Complications
items: Erosive esophagitis, peptic stricture, Barrett esophagus, adenocarcinoma
Stricture → **endoscopy + biopsy to exclude cancer**, then dilation plus acid suppression
Barrett dysplasia → endoscopic eradication; low-grade, older questions: EGD/biopsy at 6 months, even after fundoplication

rows.label: Prevention
items: Barrett screening: chronic reflux + ≥3 additional risks: male, >50, White, tobacco, obesity, first-degree family history
Smoking cessation and symptom-directed trigger reduction; routine endoscopy unnecessary for every reflux patient

rows.label: Mimics
items: Achalasia: solids and liquids dysphagia, impaired sphincter relaxation
Eosinophilic esophagitis: atopy, food impaction, eosinophilic biopsy
Functional heartburn: normal reflux burden and no symptom association

gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established ACG reflux and Barrett screening teaching.

gestational-diabetes-mellitus.name: Gestational diabetes mellitus
gestational-diabetes-mellitus.scope: Screening (50g oral glucose challenge at 24-28 weeks), diagnostic 3-hour 100g test, glycemic targets, nutritional therapy, insulin, fetal and neonatal complications (macrosomia, hypoglycemia, RDS, polycythemia)
gestational-diabetes-mellitus.core: Pregnancy-induced insulin resistance unmasks hyperglycemia, increasing fetal insulin secretion and growth; screen routinely at 24–28 weeks.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Obesity, prior GDM/macrosomia, family history of type 2 diabetes, PCOS
High-risk patients need early assessment for previously unrecognized overt diabetes

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually asymptomatic; excessive fetal growth or polyhydramnios may prompt evaluation
Early marked hyperglycemia suggests preexisting diabetes rather than typical later-onset GDM

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Placental hormones increase maternal insulin requirements; inadequate beta-cell compensation causes dysglycemia
Maternal glucose crosses placenta; insulin does not; fetal hyperinsulinemia persists briefly after birth
Fetal hyperinsulinemia → macrosomia; antagonizes cortisol → less surfactant, **RDS**

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Two-step screen: **nonfasting 50 g challenge**, 1-hour threshold 130–140 mg/dL by local protocol
Positive challenge → fasting 100 g, 3-hour OGTT; **≥2 abnormal values** diagnose GDM
Alternative one-step 75 g OGTT: fasting ≥92, 1-hour ≥180, or 2-hour ≥153 mg/dL
HbA1c alone does not replace pregnancy glucose testing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ First: **individualized nutrition, activity, home glucose monitoring**; avoid severe carbohydrate restriction
★ Targets: fasting **<95**, 1-hour <140, or 2-hour <120 mg/dL
Above targets despite lifestyle → **insulin preferred**; metformin crosses placenta, counsel if used
Medication need or poor control → fetal surveillance; delivery timing depends on control and obstetric findings
Suspected fetal weight ≥4,500 g with diabetes → discuss planned cesarean

rows.label: Complications
items: Maternal: preeclampsia, cesarean delivery, future type 2 diabetes
Fetal: macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, birth trauma; poor control increases stillbirth risk
Neonate: **hypoglycemia**, RDS, polycythemia, jaundice; congenital anomalies mainly reflect pregestational diabetes

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Postpartum **75 g OGTT at 4–12 weeks**; lifelong diabetes testing every 1–3 years
Breastfeeding, weight management, activity; most GDM insulin needs resolve after placental delivery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pregestational diabetes: overt diagnostic-range hyperglycemia early in pregnancy
Physiologic glycosuria: lower renal threshold without diagnostic blood glucose abnormalities

gestational-trophoblastic-disease.name: Gestational trophoblastic disease
gestational-trophoblastic-disease.scope: Complete hydatidiform mole, partial hydatidiform mole, choriocarcinoma, suction curettage, serial beta-hCG surveillance, contraception
gestational-trophoblastic-disease.core: Abnormal trophoblastic proliferation causes excessive hCG, bleeding, and vesicular placental tissue; persistent hCG after evacuation suggests gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior molar pregnancy, extremes of reproductive age; choriocarcinoma can follow any pregnancy

rows.label: Clues
items: Vaginal bleeding, hyperemesis, uterus larger than dates, bilateral theca lutein cysts
★ **Preeclampsia before 20 weeks** or gestational thyrotoxicosis → suspect mole
Postpregnancy bleeding with cough/hemoptysis or neurologic symptoms → metastatic trophoblastic malignancy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Abnormal fertilization produces proliferative hydropic villi; high hCG stimulates thyroid and ovarian receptors
Choriocarcinoma lacks chorionic villi and spreads hematogenously, especially to lungs, vagina, brain

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Quantitative **β-hCG + pelvic ultrasound**; snowstorm/multicystic placental appearance may be absent early
Evacuated tissue histopathology confirms; p57 absent in complete mole, retained in partial mole
★ Postevacuation **hCG plateau over 3 weeks or rise over 2 weeks** → evaluate GTN
Suspected neoplasia → chest imaging and stage/risk assessment; avoid biopsy of vascular vaginal metastasis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Stabilize bleeding → **suction curettage**; send tissue; give anti-D if Rh-negative
Hysterectomy an option when fertility not desired; surveillance remains necessary
Low-risk GTN → methotrexate or actinomycin D; high-risk → multiagent chemotherapy
hCG every 1–2 weeks until normal; partial: reconfirm after 1 month; complete: monthly for 6 months

rows.label: Complications
items: Hemorrhage, thyroid storm, early hypertensive disease, invasive mole, metastatic malignancy
Chemotherapy toxicity; prognosis often excellent even with metastatic disease when treated

rows.label: Prevention
items: Reliable contraception during hCG surveillance; combined OCPs acceptable; defer pregnancy until follow-up complete
Future pregnancy → early ultrasound and postpregnancy hCG assessment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Multiple gestation: high hCG with recognizable normally developing fetuses
Missed abortion: nonviable gestation without trophoblastic overgrowth

table.title: Molar subtypes
rows: Usually triploid; maternal + two paternal sets

gestational-trophoblastic-disease.evidence: Surveillance checked 2026-10-30: [FIGO 2025 update](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12411817/); remaining pathology established teaching.

glaucoma.name: Glaucoma
glaucoma.scope: Open-angle glaucoma, acute angle-closure glaucoma, increased intraocular pressure, optic disc cupping, tonometry, visual field testing, topical prostaglandins, laser trabeculoplasty, iridotomy
glaucoma.core: Progressive optic nerve damage threatens vision; a sudden painful red eye from angle closure is an emergency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Open-angle: older age, family history, African ancestry, myopia, chronic glucocorticoids
Angle closure: shallow chamber, hyperopia, aging lens, pharmacologic dilation

rows.label: Clues
items: Open-angle: central acuity preserved until late
★ Acute closure: halos, vomiting, hazy cornea, **fixed mid-dilated pupil**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Open-angle: trabecular outflow resistance despite patent angle
Pupillary block → bowed iris obstructs trabecular meshwork → rapid IOP rise

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Tonometry** measures IOP; normal pressure does not exclude glaucoma
**Gonioscopy** determines angle anatomy
Disc exam/OCT: increased cup-to-disc ratio, rim thinning, retinal nerve fiber loss
Automated perimetry: nasal step or arcuate scotoma; serial testing tracks progression

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute closure: urgent ophthalmology; acetazolamide plus topical timolol and brimonidine; IV mannitol if refractory
Pilocarpine after IOP falls in pupillary block; delay definitive laser until cornea clears
Open-angle progression despite maximal tolerated therapy → consider filtration surgery

rows.label: Complications
items: Irreversible optic nerve damage and blindness
Latanoprost: iris darkening and eyelash growth

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Prophylactic iridotomy in fellow eye after primary acute closure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Anterior uveitis: small pupil, consensual photophobia, anterior chamber cells
Conjunctivitis: discharge, preserved acuity, minimal pain

glaucoma.evidence: Checked AAO Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma Preferred Practice Pattern (2025).

head-and-neck-cancer.name: Head and neck cancer
head-and-neck-cancer.scope: Oral cavity cancer, laryngeal cancer, pharyngeal cancer, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, tobacco and alcohol risk, HPV-associated squamous cell carcinoma
head-and-neck-cancer.core: Persistent hoarseness, unilateral throat/ear symptoms, a nonhealing oral lesion, or an adult neck mass requires malignancy evaluation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Tobacco, alcohol: each independent, dose-dependent squamous cancer risk, synergistic together; betel nut in some populations
HPV exposure drives many oropharyngeal cancers; EBV associated with nasopharyngeal carcinoma

rows.label: Clues
items: Oral ulcer or red/white plaque persisting >2–3 weeks; dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss
★ **Adult persistent lateral neck mass** may be metastatic carcinoma, even when cystic
Unilateral referred otalgia with normal otoscopy; hemoptysis or stridor indicates advanced local disease
Nasopharyngeal disease → unilateral serous otitis, epistaxis or cranial neuropathy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mucosal squamous transformation and lymphatic spread; field carcinogenesis produces synchronous/second primary tumors

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Direct visualization and biopsy** of mucosal lesion; flexible nasolaryngoscopy for inaccessible sites
Neck mass → contrast CT/MRI plus **fine-needle aspiration**; avoid initial open biopsy
Oropharyngeal tumor → p16/HPV testing; staging imaging assesses regional nodes and distant metastases
Persistent hoarseness → laryngoscopy; no prolonged empiric reflux treatment when malignancy clues present

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Airway compromise/stridor → **secure airway** with ENT/anesthesia support
Early localized cancer → surgery or radiation according to site and function
Locally advanced → combined surgery/radiation with cisplatin-based systemic treatment or definitive chemoradiation
Nasopharyngeal cancer → chemoradiation; recurrent/metastatic disease → systemic treatment, often checkpoint inhibitor

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, airway obstruction, malnutrition, carotid bleeding; nodal/distant metastases
Radiation → xerostomia, dental decay, osteoradionecrosis; surgery → speech/swallow impairment

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Smoking/alcohol cessation, HPV vaccination; dental assessment before head/neck radiation
Swallowing rehabilitation, nutrition support; surveillance for recurrence and second primary cancer

rows.label: Mimics
items: Laryngitis: brief postviral hoarseness resolving with recovery
Branchial cleft cyst: benign developmental lesion; new adult cystic mass still needs cancer exclusion

head-and-neck-cancer.evidence: Neck-mass evaluation checked 2026-10-30: [AAO-HNS adult neck-mass guideline](https://www.entnet.org/quality-practice/quality-products/clinical-practice-guidelines/evaluation-of-the-neck-mass-in-adults/); oncology: established teaching.

heart-failure.name: Heart failure
heart-failure.scope: HFrEF, HFpEF, acute decompensated heart failure, cardiogenic flash pulmonary edema, guideline-directed medical therapy, neurohormonal activation (RAAS, ADH-mediated hyponatremia)
heart-failure.core: Inadequate cardiac output or elevated filling pressures → pulmonary or systemic congestion, even with a normal ejection fraction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: CAD, hypertension, valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, alcohol, cardiotoxic chemotherapy
Decompensation triggers: ischemia, infection, arrhythmia, missed diuretics, NSAIDs

rows.label: Clues
items: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, elevated JVP, crackles or wheeze (cardiac asthma), dependent edema
S3 suggests volume overload; S4 suggests stiff ventricle
★ **Flash edema**: abrupt respiratory distress, severe hypertension, pink frothy sputum

rows.label: Pathophys
items: RAAS/sympathetic activation → vasoconstriction, sodium retention, adverse remodeling
Low effective volume → baroreceptor-driven nonosmotic **ADH** release → dilutional hyponatremia; marker of advanced disease
Alveolar flooding → V/Q mismatch, widened A-a gradient, hypoxemia
High-output HF: severe anemia, AV fistula (larger fistula → more shunt); HF signs with **normal/high EF**

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Echocardiography**: EF, valves, wall motion; ECG, CXR, BNP support diagnosis
Low BNP argues against HF; obesity lowers BNP, renal dysfunction raises it
Identify precipitant: troponin, CBC, electrolytes, creatinine; evaluate ischemic cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute congestion → **IV furosemide**; hypoxemia → oxygen; respiratory distress → noninvasive ventilation
★ Hypertensive pulmonary edema → **IV nitroglycerin**; shock → norepinephrine ± dobutamine, urgent cause correction
Congested HFrEF → loop diuretic + **ACE inhibitor/ARNI first**; beta-blocker/MRA once compensated; ACE inhibitor → ARNI: 36-hour washout
MRA: eGFR >30, K <5; never ACE inhibitor + ARB; EF ≤35% despite GDMT → consider ICD
HFrEF foundation drugs lower mortality; loop diuretics, nitrates alone, digoxin relieve symptoms only

rows.label: Complications
items: Cardiorenal syndrome, ventricular arrhythmia, sudden death, hepatic congestion
Diuresis → hypokalemia; RAAS blockade → hyperkalemia, renal dysfunction; monitor creatinine/K

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Daily weights, sodium moderation, adherence; **continue GDMT after EF recovery**
Treat hypertension, CAD, AF; smoking cessation, exercise, influenza/pneumococcal vaccination

rows.label: Mimics
items: COPD: obstructive spirometry, hyperinflation
Nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia
PE: pleuritic pain, thrombotic risk, RV strain
ARDS: diffuse infiltrates, no cephalization; massive crystalloid + **cephalization/perihilar fullness** → volume overload

table.title: Chronic phenotypes
rows: Sacubitril/valsartan (or ACEi/ARB), carvedilol/metoprolol succinate, spironolactone, dapagliflozin

heart-failure.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACC HFrEF 2024](https://www.acc.org/Latest-in-Cardiology/ten-points-to-remember/2024/03/06/19/22/2024-acc-expert-consensus-hfref); other points established teaching.

hemolytic-anemias.name: Hemolytic Anemias
hemolytic-anemias.scope: autoimmune hemolytic anemia (warm and cold agglutinins), hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency, DAT/Coombs testing, peripheral smear, complications
hemolytic-anemias.core: Reticulocytosis, elevated LDH/indirect bilirubin and reduced haptoglobin suggest hemolysis; DAT and smear identify the mechanism.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune disease, CLL, drugs → immune hemolysis; infections can trigger cold-antibody disease
Family history → inherited membrane/enzyme defect; oxidants, fava beans or infection trigger G6PD crises
Coombs-negative newborn jaundice after maternal oxidant drug → consider G6PD; X-linked, Mediterranean ancestry

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, pallor, jaundice, dark urine; splenomegaly suggests chronic extravascular destruction
Severe intravascular lysis → hemoglobinuria, back pain, AKI; hemoglobin decline can outpace reticulocyte response
Spherocytes occur in hereditary and warm immune disease; morphology alone cannot distinguish them
Childhood gallstones + splenomegaly + family history → hereditary spherocytosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Extravascular: splenic/hepatic macrophage clearance; intravascular: RBC destruction within circulation
Free hemoglobin consumes haptoglobin; marrow compensates unless infection, deficiency or marrow failure limits production
Hereditary spherocytosis: ankyrin/spectrin cytoskeleton defect changes RBC shape → trapping in splenic red pulp

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CBC, reticulocytes, LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin**, peripheral smear
★ **DAT/Coombs** detects immune coating; negative test redirects toward nonimmune causes
Hereditary spherocytosis → eosin-5-maleimide binding test; usually normocytic, normochromic; ↑MCHC supports
G6PD activity can be falsely normal during crisis/after transfusion → repeat after recovery
Schistocytes → evaluate microangiopathy/mechanical destruction urgently, including platelet count and renal function

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe symptomatic anemia → **transfuse promptly** with blood-bank coordination; do not await perfect compatibility
Warm AIHA → glucocorticoids; refractory → rituximab or selected splenectomy
Cold disease → warmth, treat cause; rituximab-based treatment when symptomatic; steroids usually ineffective
G6PD → stop oxidant, treat trigger, supportive transfusion when severe
Hereditary spherocytosis → folate; selected severe disease → splenectomy after immunization

rows.label: Complications
items: Pigment gallstones, folate deficiency, aplastic crisis; chronic immune disease increases thrombosis risk
Splenectomy → encapsulated infection and thrombosis; intravascular disease → renal injury

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ G6PD: avoid **dapsone, primaquine, rasburicase, sulfonamides** and other oxidants
Before splenectomy: pneumococcal/meningococcal/Hib vaccines; infection education and selected antibiotic prophylaxis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Blood loss: reticulocytosis without hemolytic chemistry
Gilbert syndrome: isolated indirect bilirubin without anemia

table.title: Mechanism signatures
rows: Bite cells; Heinz bodies on supravital stain

hemolytic-anemias.evidence: Not checked online; established hematology teaching.

hereditary-hemorrhagic-telangiectasia.name: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia
hereditary-hemorrhagic-telangiectasia.scope: Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome, recurrent epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasias, pulmonary arteriovenous malformations, hepatic AVMs, cerebral AVMs, iron deficiency anemia, polycythemia
hereditary-hemorrhagic-telangiectasia.core: Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome: recurrent spontaneous nosebleeds with mucocutaneous telangiectasias and visceral arteriovenous malformations.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autosomal dominant inheritance; affected parent or other first-degree relative

rows.label: Clues
items: Blanching lesions on lips, tongue, oral mucosa and fingertips
Pulmonary involvement: exertional dyspnea, hypoxemia, clubbing, secondary erythrocytosis
Chronic nasal or GI blood loss → iron deficiency anemia

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Disordered TGF-β signaling impairs vascular development; direct arteriovenous connections bypass capillary beds

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Curaçao criteria**: core triad plus affected first-degree relative; ≥3 definite, 2 possible
★ Pulmonary screen: **agitated-saline contrast echo** → chest CT to define treatable AVMs
Brain MRI for cerebral AVMs; offer liver AVM screening in adults, preferably Doppler ultrasound
CBC and ferritin; genetic testing for uncertain diagnosis or cascade testing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Treat suitable pulmonary AVMs with **transcatheter embolization**
Nasal humidification → tranexamic acid or ENT ablation for persistent bleeding; iron replacement
Complicated hepatic AVMs → specialty care; avoid hepatic artery embolization

rows.label: Complications
items: ★ Pulmonary right-to-left shunt → paradoxical embolic stroke or brain abscess
Hepatic shunting → high-output heart failure; cerebral AVM rupture → intracranial hemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Pulmonary AVMs: antibiotic prophylaxis for bacteremia-producing procedures, meticulous IV air precautions, avoid scuba diving
Screen at-risk relatives, including children, before symptoms develop

rows.label: Mimics
items: Von Willebrand disease: mucosal bleeding without typical telangiectasias or visceral shunts
CREST: telangiectasias with Raynaud phenomenon and sclerodactyly

hereditary-hemorrhagic-telangiectasia.evidence: Checked International HHT Guidelines, including the 2020 update.

hyperbilirubinemia.name: Hyperbilirubinemia
hyperbilirubinemia.scope: Gilbert syndrome, Crigler-Najjar, Dubin-Johnson, Rotor, unconjugated vs conjugated, biliary atresia
hyperbilirubinemia.core: Fractionate bilirubin first: indirect elevation reflects production or conjugation problems; direct elevation requires assessment of hepatobiliary excretion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Fasting, illness or dehydration triggers Gilbert jaundice; family history suggests inherited bilirubin disorders
Persistent infant jaundice can reflect biliary atresia even after initially reassuring appearance

rows.label: Clues
items: Indirect bilirubin is albumin-bound and absent from urine; direct bilirubin can darken urine
★ Infant **pale/acholic stools**, dark urine, hepatomegaly → obstructive cholestasis
Pruritus, pale stools and elevated alkaline phosphatase suggest impaired bile flow
Severe neonatal indirect elevation with lethargy, poor feeding or abnormal tone → bilirubin neurotoxicity

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Heme breakdown yields unconjugated pigment; hepatic UGT conjugation enables biliary elimination
Unbound unconjugated bilirubin crosses the immature blood–brain barrier; conjugated bilirubin does not cause kernicterus
Large hematoma/cephalhematoma resorption → bilirubin overproduction, indirect jaundice

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Total/direct bilirubin**, AST/ALT, alkaline phosphatase/GGT; CBC/reticulocytes/LDH for suspected hemolysis
Isolated mild indirect elevation with normal liver tests and no hemolysis → Gilbert diagnosis
★ Jaundice beyond 2 weeks → fractionate; **direct ≥1 mg/dL at 2–4 weeks** → urgent referral
Infant cholestasis → ultrasound; biliary atresia assessment may require biopsy and operative cholangiography
Adult conjugated elevation with pain/obstruction → RUQ ultrasound before advanced duct imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected biliary atresia → urgent pediatric hepatology/surgery; **early Kasai portoenterostomy**
Severe neonatal indirect, even Coombs-positive → **phototherapy** first; exchange: failure, critical level, encephalopathy
Crigler–Najjar I → intensive phototherapy, definitive liver transplant; type II responds to phenobarbital
Gilbert, Dubin–Johnson and Rotor → reassurance once competing pathology excluded
Cholestasis → nutritional support, fat-soluble vitamins and cause-specific treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Indirect neonatal hyperbilirubinemia → acute encephalopathy/kernicterus
Untreated atresia → cirrhosis, portal hypertension, liver failure

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Inspect stool color and fractionate persistent infant jaundice; never label conjugated jaundice physiologic

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hemolysis: anemia, reticulocytosis, low haptoglobin; newborn ABO: mother O, baby A/B, Coombs-positive
Choledochal cyst: cystic/dilated extrahepatic ducts on ultrasound
Physiologic jaundice: indirect, after 24 h, peaks days 3–5, thriving; transient UGT immaturity
Breast-milk jaundice: indirect, thriving; direct elevation excludes it

hyperbilirubinemia.evidence: Infant referral checked 2026-10-30: [AAP 2025](https://publications.aap.org/aapnews/news/pdfDownload/31302); inherited syndromes established teaching.

hyperglycemic-crises.name: Hyperglycemic crises
hyperglycemic-crises.core: Insulin-deficient diabetes with osmotic diuresis: rapid acidotic illness or slowly progressive hyperosmolar encephalopathy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Infection, missed insulin, pump failure, MI; DKA often type 1, HHS often older type 2
Euglycemic triggers: **SGLT2 inhibitors**, pregnancy, fasting

rows.label: Clues
items: Polyuria, thirst, weight loss, dry mucosa, tachycardia
DKA: abdominal pain, vomiting, **Kussmaul (deep) breathing**; HHS: profound dehydration, focal deficits
★ Severe: **hypotension, stupor**, or coma → ICU

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Insulin deficit + counterregulatory hormones → lipolysis, ketogenesis; residual insulin in HHS limits ketosis
Total-body K depleted despite initially normal/high serum K

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Glucose, electrolytes, venous pH, β-hydroxybutyrate**, osmolality; ECG + trigger evaluation
Effective osmolality = 2 × Na + glucose/18; glucose in mg/dL
★ HHS: **effective osmolality >300 OR total >320 mOsm/kg**; substantial ketosis/acidosis → mixed DKA/HHS
DKA resolution: ketones <0.6 mmol/L AND (pH ≥7.3 OR HCO₃ ≥18); urine ketones/anion gap misleading

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **IV isotonic crystalloid → K correction → IV regular insulin**; K <3.5 mmol/L → delay insulin
Replace K when <5 mmol/L; glucose checks every 1–2 h, electrolytes/pH/ketones every 4 h
★ Add **dextrose** below glucose 250; euglycemic presentation → immediately; continue insulin until crisis resolves
SC basal insulin overlaps infusion 1–2 h; bicarbonate only consider pH <7.0; HHS: slower osmolar correction

rows.label: Complications
items: AKI, thrombosis; treatment: hypoglycemia, hypokalemic arrhythmias, cerebral edema (Cushing triad), hyperchloremic acidosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Sick-day fluids/ketone checks; continue basal insulin; ensure supplies and early follow-up
Hold SGLT2 inhibitors during acute illness and before surgery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Alcoholic ketoacidosis: binge then poor intake; usually no diabetes
Starvation ketosis: usually milder acidosis, no marked hyperglycemia
Toxic alcohols: osmolar gap, exposure; absent substantial ketonemia

table.title: Biochemistry; ketones and HCO₃ in mmol/L

hyperthyroidism.name: Hyperthyroidism and thyrotoxicosis
hyperthyroidism.scope: Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma, subacute thyroiditis, thyroid storm, beta-blockers, thionamides, radioactive iodine
hyperthyroidism.core: Excess circulating thyroid hormone → heat intolerance, weight loss despite appetite, tremor, and tachycardia; hormone overproduction differs from destructive release.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune history, female sex; older age favors autonomous nodules
Iodine load, amiodarone, exogenous thyroid hormone; infection/surgery can precipitate storm

rows.label: Clues
items: Hyperreflexia, lid lag, onycholysis, frequent stools, proximal weakness, widened pulse pressure; older adults: apathetic
★ **Thyroid storm**: fever, delirium, severe tachyarrhythmia, vomiting, heart failure; clinical diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Increased tissue metabolic activity and beta-adrenergic sensitivity explain systemic manifestations
Thionamides block thyroid peroxidase; PTU also reduces peripheral T4 → T3 conversion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TSH first → free T4**, total T3 if T4 normal; suppressed TSH with elevated hormones
TRAb establishes Graves; uncertain cause → **Doppler ultrasound** or radioiodine uptake (not if pregnant/lactating)
Low uptake: thyroiditis/exogenous hormone; low thyroglobulin supports exogenous ingestion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptom control: **propranolol**; caution in asthma or decompensated HF
★ Storm → ICU, cooling/fluids, beta-blockade if tolerated, **PTU → iodine ≥1 hour later**, hydrocortisone
Radioiodine contraindicated during pregnancy/lactation; significant active orbitopathy favors another definitive treatment
Compression/suspicious nodule → thyroidectomy after control; pregnancy: first-trimester PTU, later methimazole

rows.label: Complications
items: AF, embolism, osteoporosis, mild hypercalcemia, cardiomyopathy; radioiodine often → hypothyroidism
★ Thionamides: **fever/sore throat → stop drug, urgent CBC**; PTU → severe hepatotoxicity
Pregnancy: thionamides/TRAb cross placenta → **fetal goiter**, impaired swallowing, polyhydramnios

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor free T4 early during treatment; TSH recovery lags
Smoking cessation for orbitopathy; definitive treatment before planned pregnancy when feasible

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic disorder: episodic symptoms without thyroid biochemical abnormalities
Pheochromocytoma: paroxysmal headache, sweating, severe hypertension
Menopause: hot flashes with menstrual transition, normal thyroid testing
Orbital pseudotumor: involves muscle bellies and tendons; Graves spares tendons

table.title: Etiology determines treatment
rows: Diffuse uptake; bruit, orbitopathy, pretibial myxedema, acropachy (clubbing)
One hot nodule, suppressed surrounding tissue
NSAID; prednisone if severe; no thionamides

hypocalcemia.name: Hypocalcemia
hypocalcemia.scope: Hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, post-thyroidectomy, hypomagnesemia
hypocalcemia.core: Low ionized calcium causes neuromuscular irritability and QT prolongation; severe symptoms require IV calcium while the cause is corrected.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Thyroid/parathyroid surgery, autoimmune hypoparathyroidism, DiGeorge syndrome
Vitamin D deficiency from low intake, malabsorption, limited sun; CKD, pancreatitis, massive citrate transfusion
Severe hypomagnesemia from alcoholism, diarrhea, PPIs, diuretics; bisphosphonates/denosumab can precipitate deficiency

rows.label: Clues
items: Perioral tingling, distal paresthesias, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm
★ **Trousseau sign**: cuff-induced carpal spasm; Chvostek sign is less specific
★ Severe: **seizures, laryngospasm, arrhythmias**; ECG shows prolonged QT
Post-thyroidectomy tingling or stridor requires immediate calcium assessment rather than simple reassurance

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced extracellular calcium lowers nerve excitation threshold; myocardial repolarization is prolonged
Low magnesium impairs both PTH secretion and action, making calcium replacement alone ineffective

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Ionized calcium**, Mg, phosphate, creatinine, PTH, 25-hydroxyvitamin D
Low albumin lowers total calcium, not necessarily ionized; correction formulas unreliable in critical illness
Alkalosis increases albumin binding → symptomatic low ionized calcium despite unchanged total concentration
Interpret PTH relative to calcium: normal PTH can be inappropriately low during hypocalcemia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic, severe, or ECG changes → **IV calcium gluconate with ECG monitoring**
Mild stable disease → oral calcium; nutritional vitamin D deficiency → cholecalciferol/ergocalciferol
Hypoparathyroidism or advanced CKD → **calcitriol** plus calcium; coordinate phosphate management
★ **Replace magnesium** when deficient; correct underlying cause, avoid overcorrection

rows.label: Complications
items: Tetany, seizures, ventricular arrhythmias; chronic deficiency can cause cataracts and basal ganglia calcification
Overreplacement → hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis; monitor serum and urine calcium

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor calcium after neck surgery and antiresorptive treatment; ensure sufficient vitamin D/calcium intake
Chronic hypoparathyroidism: target symptom control with low-normal serum calcium, avoiding renal calcium loading

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperventilation syndrome: transient alkalosis-related ionized reduction; assess precipitating illness
Seizure disorder: no biochemical calcium explanation; pseudohypocalcemia: normal ionized level

hypocalcemia.evidence: Not checked online; established endocrine teaching.

hypothesis-testing-and-statistical-tests.name: Hypothesis testing and statistical tests
hypothesis-testing-and-statistical-tests.scope: Null and alternative hypotheses, Type I and Type II errors, statistical power, confidence intervals, p-values, t-tests (paired, unpaired), ANOVA, chi-square, Pearson correlation
hypothesis-testing-and-statistical-tests.core: Hypothesis tests quantify incompatibility with a null model; confidence intervals describe effect estimates and uncertainty.

rows.label: Definition
items: H0: no difference/association; H1: specified difference or association
★ **α**: false-positive probability; Type I error rejects a true null
★ **β**: false-negative probability; Type II error misses a real effect

rows.label: Formula
items: Power = **1 − β**; increases with sample size, effect size, α, lower variability
95% CI ≈ estimate ± 1.96 × standard error; plausible range for true effect

rows.label: Interpret
items: ★ **p-value**: probability of equally/more extreme data assuming H0; not probability H0 true
95% CI excludes 0 for differences or 1 for ratios → two-sided p <0.05

rows.label: Use when
items: Pearson r: linear association between continuous variables; range −1 to +1
Ordinal/non-normal independent data → Mann–Whitney; paired → Wilcoxon signed-rank

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Nonsignificant ≠ equivalent; statistical significance ≠ clinical importance
Repeated comparisons inflate false positives; prespecify outcomes or adjust α
Correlation neither establishes causation nor detects every nonlinear relationship

hypothesis-testing-and-statistical-tests.evidence: Statistical definitions; no clinical guideline involved.

infective-endocarditis.name: Infective endocarditis
infective-endocarditis.scope: Native and prosthetic valve endocarditis, Duke criteria, prophylaxis, IV drug use endocarditis, blood culture diagnostic criteria
infective-endocarditis.core: Persistent bacteremia with valve infection causes systemic emboli, valve destruction, and immune-complex injury.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prosthetic valve, prior endocarditis, congenital valve abnormality, intracardiac device
Injection drug use → tricuspid involvement; healthcare exposure, indwelling vascular access

rows.label: Clues
items: Fever, new regurgitant murmur, embolic stroke, splenic infarct, hematuria
Janeway lesions painless; Osler nodes painful; Roth spots retinal; splinter hemorrhages nonspecific
★ **New conduction block** → periannular abscess; right-sided disease → septic pulmonary emboli

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Endothelial injury → platelet-fibrin nidus → microbial adherence and vegetation
Immune complexes → glomerulonephritis; infected fragments disseminate through downstream circulation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Three blood-culture sets before antibiotics**; separate peripheral draws unless resuscitation would be delayed
Major microbiology: **typical organism in ≥2 culture sets**, nontypical in ≥3; specialized serology/PCR also qualifies
★ **TTE → TEE** if prosthesis/high suspicion; major imaging: vegetation, abscess, perforation, new significant regurgitation
Definite clinical Duke: 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria
Minor: predisposition, fever, vascular phenomena, immunologic phenomena, nondiagnostic microbiology

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Empiric **IV vancomycin + cefepime** for acutely ill/healthcare-associated cases; tailor to cultures and setting
MSSA → nafcillin/oxacillin or cefazolin; susceptible viridans streptococci → ceftriaxone
Prolonged pathogen-directed IV antibiotics; prosthetic infections need specialist regimen and early surgical evaluation
Surgery: heart failure, abscess, persistent bacteremia, fungal infection, or selected recurrent/large embolizing vegetations

rows.label: Complications
items: Acute regurgitation, heart failure, mycotic aneurysm, metastatic infection
Antibiotic nephrotoxicity, line infection; hemorrhage into embolic cerebral lesions

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Dental **amoxicillin** for prosthetic valve/material, previous IE, selected cyanotic/residual CHD, transplant valvulopathy
Good oral hygiene, sterile access; no routine prophylaxis for GI/GU procedures or isolated MVP

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis: cancer/autoimmune disease, sterile cultures
Atrial myxoma: positional obstruction, intracavitary mass; vasculitis: no infected vegetation

inflammatory-bowel-disease.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
inflammatory-bowel-disease.scope: Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, extraintestinal manifestations (erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, uveitis), toxic megacolon, colorectal cancer risk, biologic therapy
inflammatory-bowel-disease.core: Chronic relapsing intestinal inflammation: Crohn disease affects any gastrointestinal segment; ulcerative colitis begins in the rectum.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, young adulthood; smoking worsens Crohn disease
NSAIDs and enteric infections can precipitate flares

rows.label: Clues
items: Chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, anemia; children may have growth failure
Arthritis, uveitis; PSC particularly associated with UC
Erythema nodosum: tender nonulcerating nodules; **pyoderma gangrenosum**: rapid painful violaceous ulcer, purulent base
★ Severe colitis: fever, tachycardia, frequent bloody stools; distention, colon >6 cm → **toxic megacolon**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dysregulated mucosal immune response to intestinal microbiota in genetically susceptible hosts

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stool **C. difficile** testing and cultures before attributing worsening diarrhea to inflammation
Fecal calprotectin supports intestinal inflammation; **ileocolonoscopy with biopsies** confirms
Suspected small-bowel disease or abscess → CT/MR enterography; avoid capsule with suspected stricture
Partial SBO, suspected stricture → enterography; older exam questions may expect **water-soluble small-bowel follow-through**
Fulminant colitis → abdominal radiograph and limited sigmoidoscopy; avoid full colonoscopy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute severe UC → hospitalization, **IV methylprednisolone**, fluids, VTE prophylaxis
Steroid-refractory severe UC → infliximab or cyclosporine; perforation or megacolon → urgent colectomy
★ Moderate/severe flare without obstruction or abscess → **prednisone** induces remission only; **never maintenance**
Crohn abscess → antibiotics and drainage before immunosuppression
UC with colorectal cancer → **total proctocolectomy**, not segmental colectomy

rows.label: Complications
items: Fistulas (enterovaginal → vaginal flatus), strictures, obstruction in Crohn; colectomy does not cure Crohn
Terminal ileal Crohn → B12 deficiency, **bile salt malabsorption** → steatorrhea
Colonic disease → colorectal cancer; active inflammation → venous thromboembolism

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Colonic disease → surveillance colonoscopy beginning about **8 years** after onset; PSC → immediately
Vaccinate and screen TB/HBV before biologics; smoking cessation for Crohn

rows.label: Mimics
items: IBS: no bleeding, weight loss or inflammatory markers
Ischemic colitis: abrupt pain followed by hematochezia, vascular risk

table.title: Distribution and outpatient treatment
rows: RLQ mass, cobblestones, perianal disease, granulomas
Bloody diarrhea, tenesmus; friability, crypt abscesses, pseudopolyps

informed-consent-and-capacity.name: Informed consent and capacity
informed-consent-and-capacity.scope: Decision-making capacity, informed consent, emergency exception (implied consent), refusal of treatment, AMA discharge
informed-consent-and-capacity.core: A capable adult may accept or refuse treatment after understanding its benefits, material risks, alternatives, and consequences of refusal.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ Capacity: **understand, appreciate (own case), reason, communicate**; decision-specific, fluctuating
Competence: legal; diagnosis, age, alcohol use, incarceration, disagreement alone ≠ incapacity

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Explain benefits, material risks, alternatives/no treatment; **qualified interpreter and teach-back**
Correct delirium, intoxication, pain, communication barriers; reassess capacity
AMA request: assess capacity, explore barriers, offer safer plan, document discussion and follow-up

rows.label: Don't
items: Capable refusal → respect choice, even if life-saving or pregnant; avoid coercion, abandonment
No valid consent → possible **battery**; signed form alone insufficient
Refusing one therapy (blood) ≠ refusing all; provide other indicated care, including surgery

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Emergency + incapacity + no surrogate/directive/verified refusal → implied consent to treat
★ Parents refuse minor's life-saving transfusion → **treat emergency**; seek court authority if feasible
Incapacity without emergency → authorized surrogate; involve patient to remaining ability

rows.label: Traps
items: Psychiatric illness does not automatically remove capacity; assess the specific decision
Suicide danger may justify protective detention despite expressed desire to leave
New material procedure or changed risk → renewed consent; consent revocable anytime before procedure

table.title: Who decides
rows: Ask whom to involve; facilitate promptly; no override
Minor decides; no parental consent (state law varies)
Parents seek unproven remedy for child
Continue proven therapy; investigate remedy; CPS not first
Close; discuss after waking; no next-of-kin consent
Autonomy ≠ entitlement; physician refuses, explains, offers alternatives

informed-consent-and-capacity.evidence: Not checked online; established consent/capacity ethics; emergency and minor-consent law varies by jurisdiction.

inherited-bleeding-disorders.name: Inherited bleeding disorders
inherited-bleeding-disorders.scope: Hemophilia A, Hemophilia B, von Willebrand disease, factor XI deficiency, hemarthrosis, mixing studies, factor VIII inhibitors
inherited-bleeding-disorders.core: Deep tissue bleeding suggests a coagulation-factor defect; mucosal bleeding suggests platelet/von Willebrand dysfunction, even with a normal platelet count.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hemophilia A/B: X-linked, usually males; maternal family history may be absent
vWD usually autosomal dominant; factor XI deficiency autosomal, enriched in Ashkenazi ancestry

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Recurrent **hemarthroses**, muscle hematomas and delayed postoperative bleeding → hemophilia
Epistaxis, gingival bleeding, easy bruising and heavy menses → vWD
Factor XI deficiency: variable postsurgical bleeding, especially oral/urologic procedures; hemarthrosis uncommon
Unexpected major bleeding after circumcision or surgery may reveal previously undiagnosed disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: VIII/IX/XI deficits impair intrinsic-pathway thrombin generation and fibrin stabilization
vWF mediates platelet adhesion and stabilizes factor VIII; deficiency impairs primary and sometimes secondary hemostasis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ CBC/platelets, PT, aPTT; **mixing study corrects** factor deficiency, fails with inhibitor
Factor VIII, IX or XI activity identifies deficiency; hemophilia generally normal PT/platelets
★ Suspected vWD → **vWF antigen, activity and factor VIII**; aPTT may be normal
Stress, pregnancy and estrogen raise vWF; repeat borderline testing when clinically stable
Severe hemophilia: factor activity <1%; inhibitor testing if replacement response is inadequate

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Major suspected hemophilic bleeding → **replace deficient factor immediately**, before imaging delays
Hemophilia A → factor VIII; B → factor IX; emicizumab prophylaxis for selected A
Mild responsive A or type 1 vWD → **desmopressin after response testing**
Severe vWD → vWF-containing concentrate; avoid desmopressin in type 2B and ineffective type 3
Mucosal bleeding → tranexamic acid; factor XI procedures → antifibrinolytic ± plasma with hematology planning

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic hemarthropathy, intracranial hemorrhage, anemia; factor inhibitors complicate replacement
Desmopressin → water retention/hyponatremia; factor concentrates can increase thrombosis risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Individualized factor/nonfactor prophylaxis, dental care, procedure planning; avoid aspirin and nonselective NSAIDs
Family genetic counseling; fluid restriction and sodium monitoring around desmopressin

rows.label: Mimics
items: ITP: low platelets with mucocutaneous bleeding
Acquired factor VIII inhibitor: new bleeding, mixing fails to correct
Vitamin K deficiency: PT prolonged first

insomnia.name: Insomnia
insomnia.scope: Chronic insomnia, sleep hygiene, stimulus control therapy, sleep restriction, delayed sleep-wake phase disorder, pharmacotherapy indications
insomnia.core: Persistent difficulty sleeping despite adequate opportunity, with daytime impairment, calls for CBT-I and evaluation of perpetuating causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Stress, depression/anxiety, chronic pain, irregular schedules, conditioned worry about sleep
Caffeine, alcohol, nicotine, stimulants, glucocorticoids; older age and menopause

rows.label: Clues
items: Difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep or early awakening, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability
★ Chronic disorder: **≥3 nights/week for ≥3 months**, with adequate sleep opportunity
Delayed phase: late sleep/wake times but normal sleep quality and duration when schedule unrestricted
Loud snoring, witnessed apnea, irresistible sleepiness, or restless legs suggests another sleep disorder

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cognitive/physiologic hyperarousal and learned bed–wake association perpetuate insomnia
Circadian phase delay misaligns internal timing with required social schedule

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Sleep history and 1–2-week diary**; review schedule, substances, mood, pain, and medications
Polysomnography: suspected apnea, limb movements, unusual behaviors, or refractory uncertainty; not routine
Actigraphy can clarify circadian timing; assess bipolar disorder before sleep-restriction interventions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **CBT-I first-line**: stimulus control, sleep restriction/compression, cognitive restructuring, relaxation
Stimulus control: bed only for sleep/sex; leave when persistently awake, return when sleepy
Restrict time in bed to consolidate sleep, then expand; fixed wake time and avoid naps
★ **Sleep hygiene alone insufficient**; reduce evening stimulants, alcohol, screens; dark quiet room
Short-term: doxepin, ramelteon, orexin antagonist; acute stressor → **zolpidem**; maintenance + dysphoria → **trazodone**

rows.label: Complications
items: Impaired driving/work, low mood; hypnotics, especially benzodiazepines (alprazolam) → falls, cognitive impairment, dependence
Z-drugs can cause complex sleep behaviors; avoid sedative combinations and routine antihistamines in older adults

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain regular wake time and daytime activity; address pain/mood disorders and relapse triggers
★ Delayed phase → **fixed daily bed and wake times**, morning bright light, evening melatonin, gradual advance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Insufficient sleep: inadequate opportunity, improves with longer sleep duration
Mania: reduced need for sleep with increased energy, rather than distressing fatigue
OSA: sleep fragmentation with snoring/apneas; coexistence possible

interstitial-lung-disease.name: Interstitial lung disease
interstitial-lung-disease.scope: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, sarcoidosis, pneumoconioses, restrictive PFTs (reduced DLCO, normal/high FEV1/FVC), high-resolution CT
interstitial-lung-disease.core: Progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, and inspiratory crackles suggest diffuse parenchymal lung disease; HRCT patterns and exposure history identify the cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age >60 and smoking: IPF; autoimmune disease; familial fibrosis
Amiodarone, bleomycin, nitrofurantoin; occupational silica/coal/asbestos, organic antigens; prior thoracic radiation

rows.label: Clues
items: Fine basal Velcro crackles, exertional desaturation, later clubbing; systemic rheumatic features can reveal cause
Sarcoidosis: bilateral hilar adenopathy, uveitis, erythema nodosum, sometimes hypercalcemia
Rapidly worsening oxygenation → infection, embolism, edema, or acute exacerbation evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alveolar/interstitial injury and aberrant repair reduce lung compliance and gas-transfer capacity
Granulomatous inflammation or fibrogenic dust responses produce distinct imaging distributions

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **HRCT + full PFTs** after chest radiograph; obtain detailed drug, occupation, hobby, autoimmune history
★ **↓TLC, ↓DLCO, normal/↑FEV1/FVC** support restriction; low FVC alone is insufficient
UIP: basal subpleural reticulation, traction bronchiectasis, honeycombing; exclude known causes before labeling IPF
Autoantibodies when connective-tissue disease suspected; BAL/biopsy selected through multidisciplinary review
Typical UIP without secondary cause may avoid surgical biopsy; assess exertional oxygen needs

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Remove offending exposure/drug**, pulmonary rehabilitation, oxygen for hypoxemia; treat identified cause
★ IPF: **nintedanib or pirfenidone** slows decline; no routine chronic prednisone-based immunosuppression
Inflammatory sarcoid/autoimmune disease: selected steroids or steroid-sparing agents; mild sarcoid may need observation
Progressive fibrotic non-IPF disease → nintedanib consideration; advanced disease → early transplant evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, respiratory failure, exacerbations; asbestos raises lung cancer/mesothelioma risk
Silicosis increases TB susceptibility; antifibrotics can cause GI adverse effects and liver injury

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, respiratory immunizations, occupational dust controls, medication monitoring; follow FVC/DLCO trends

rows.label: Mimics
items: Heart failure: congestion/cardiomegaly, volume response; emphysema: obstruction with hyperinflation
Neuromuscular restriction: low volumes with relatively preserved diffusion capacity

table.title: Imaging clues to etiology
rows: Centrilobular nodules, mosaic attenuation, air trapping

ischemic-stroke-and-tia.name: Ischemic stroke and TIA
ischemic-stroke-and-tia.scope: TIA (including amaurosis fugax), ischemic stroke, acute management (tPA, thrombectomy), secondary prevention, risk factors
ischemic-stroke-and-tia.core: Abrupt focal neurologic loss from cerebral ischemia; transient monocular blindness means retinal embolism from the ipsilateral carotid.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Hypertension: greatest modifiable risk factor**; smoking, diabetes, dyslipidemia, carotid atherosclerosis
Atrial fibrillation, recent MI, endocarditis, arterial dissection

rows.label: Clues
items: **Broca** nonfluent, poor repetition, intact comprehension; **Wernicke** fluent paraphasias, poor comprehension, no insight
Crossed: **Weber** ipsilateral CN III, contralateral hemiparesis (midbrain); lateral pons: ipsilateral full-face palsy, deafness
★ **Last known well** establishes treatment timing; symptom discovery time may differ
TIA: resolved deficit without acute infarction, often embolic; urgent evaluation despite normal examination

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Thromboembolism or small-vessel occlusion → infarct core surrounded by salvageable penumbra
Reperfusion preserves threatened tissue but increases hemorrhagic transformation risk

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Fingerstick glucose + **noncontrast head CT** first; normal early CT does not exclude ischemia
CTA head/neck for large-vessel occlusion; MRI diffusion for small infarcts or diagnostic uncertainty
ECG, telemetry, carotid imaging; echocardiography for suspected cardiac emboli

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling deficit, eligible ≤4.5 hours → **alteplase or tenecteplase**; imaging-selected extended windows possible
Thrombolysis: BP <185/110 before, <180/105 after; exclude bleeding and significant anticoagulant effect
★ Large-vessel occlusion → **mechanical thrombectomy**, selected cases through 24 hours; do not delay thrombolysis
No reperfusion: generally allow BP ≤220/120; oxygen for hypoxemia; swallow assessment before oral intake
Aspirin after hemorrhage excluded; after thrombolysis, wait 24 hours and repeat imaging

rows.label: Complications
items: Cerebral edema, aspiration, venous thrombosis, seizures, disability

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Minor noncardioembolic stroke/high-risk TIA → short **aspirin + clopidogrel**, then single antiplatelet
AF/cardioembolic → oral anticoagulation, timing by infarct/bleeding risk; noncardioembolic → antiplatelet only
Symptomatic carotid stenosis 70–99% → endarterectomy when eligible; selected 50–69% also benefit
Long-term antiplatelet (aspirin allergy → clopidogrel); undertreated hypertension → **intensify antihypertensives**; high-intensity statin

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hypoglycemia: deficit reverses with glucose
Migraine aura: spreading positive symptoms; seizure: witnessed convulsion followed by Todd paralysis

table.title: Vascular localization
rows: Occipital: contralateral homonymous hemianopia; macular sparing
Diplopia, vertigo, dysarthria, ataxia, crossed/bilateral signs, coma
Vertigo; ipsilateral Horner/face/ataxia/palate; contralateral body pain-temperature

juvenile-idiopathic-arthritis.name: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis
juvenile-idiopathic-arthritis.scope: Oligoarticular JIA, polyarticular JIA, systemic JIA, uveitis screening, NSAIDs, methotrexate
juvenile-idiopathic-arthritis.core: Persistent childhood inflammatory arthritis is a diagnosis of exclusion; silent eye disease and systemic inflammatory complications require active surveillance.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Onset before age 16; female predominance in oligoarticular/polyarticular forms
Young onset, ANA positivity and oligoarthritis increase chronic anterior uveitis risk

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Morning stiffness, swollen joints or painless limp** persisting ≥6 weeks
Limited range of motion, warmth, leg-length difference; child may avoid activity rather than report pain
Systemic inflammation with falling platelets, hepatic dysfunction or altered mentation → macrophage activation syndrome

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune-mediated synovitis → cartilage damage and altered growth
Systemic form predominantly autoinflammatory, involving IL-1 and IL-6 pathways

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis after excluding infection/malignancy**; CBC, ESR/CRP, ANA, RF by phenotype
ANA predicts eye risk rather than proving arthritis; RF often negative
Acutely hot painful joint with fever → arthrocentesis/culture before attributing to JIA
Suspected macrophage activation → ferritin, triglycerides, fibrinogen, CBC and liver enzymes

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Oligoarthritis → **NSAIDs or intra-articular glucocorticoid**; persistent disease → methotrexate
Polyarthritis → methotrexate; uncontrolled disease → biologic such as TNF inhibitor
★ Systemic JIA → **IL-1/IL-6 inhibitor** such as anakinra/tocilizumab; limit chronic systemic steroids
Uveitis → topical ocular steroid, then methotrexate/adalimumab for persistent disease; avoid etanercept for ocular control
Physical rehabilitation, range-of-motion exercises and nutrition support

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic uveitis → cataract, glaucoma, vision loss without symptoms; joint destruction and growth disturbances
Macrophage activation → cytopenias, coagulopathy, multiorgan failure; immunosuppression → infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Slit-lamp screening**, every 3 months in high-risk children, even without eye complaints
Vaccination review, TB screening before biologics; monitor methotrexate CBC/liver tests

rows.label: Mimics
items: Septic arthritis: abrupt severe monoarthritis, bacterial culture
Leukemia: nocturnal bone pain, cytopenias/blasts; reactive arthritis: follows infection, usually self-limited
Acute rheumatic fever: recent strep, migratory arthritis, carditis, nodules; not persistent single-joint swelling

knee-injuries.name: Knee injuries
knee-injuries.scope: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear, posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) tear, collateral ligaments, meniscal tears, knee dislocation, popliteal artery injury, Ottawa knee rules
knee-injuries.core: Knee trauma assessment starts with neurovascular safety and fracture risk, then uses mechanism, effusion timing, and targeted ligament or meniscal tests.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pivoting/cutting sports, contact trauma, dashboard impact, hyperextension
Older age, osteoporosis, and inability to bear weight increase fracture probability

rows.label: Clues
items: Immediate large effusion suggests hemarthrosis; delayed swelling and catching suggest meniscal injury
★ **Gross deformity or spontaneously reduced dislocation** → popliteal artery injury risk
Cool foot, weak pulses, paresthesia, escalating pain → vascular compromise or compartment syndrome

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ligament disruption → instability; displaced meniscal fragment → mechanical locking
Knee dislocation may stretch/tear popliteal artery despite restored alignment and initially palpable pulses

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Neurovascular examination before and after reduction**; ABI assesses arterial injury
★ ABI **<0.9, abnormal pulses, or pre-reduction deficit → CT angiography**; hard ischemic signs → vascular intervention
Normal ABI/pulses, no prior deficit → serial vascular checks, not immediate discharge
Ottawa: age ≥55, isolated patellar/fibular-head tenderness, flexion <90°, or inability four-step weight-bearing → radiographs
MRI for soft-tissue injury after fracture evaluation; locked knee → prompt orthopedic assessment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Dislocation → **urgent reduction before angiography**, immobilization, orthopedic/vascular consultation
Initial sprain → ice/compression, analgesia, protected weight bearing then early rehabilitation
